title: CHRISTIAN MARRIAGE DOES NOT MEAN UNLIMITED SEXUAL ENTITLEMENT
paragraphs:
CHRISTIAN MARRIAGE DOES NOT MEAN UNLIMITED SEXUAL ENTITLEMENT
A Wedding Ring Is Not a Lifetime Permission Slip to Ignore Your Spouse’s Pain — and the Gospel Never Turns Covenant Love Into a License to Take
There are wounds that happen outside marriage.
And then there are wounds that happen in the very place where someone believed they would finally be safe.
That second kind can be harder to explain.
Because what do you say when the person hurting you is the person who prayed beside you at the altar?
What do you call it when Scripture is hanging on the bedroom wall, wedding photographs are smiling from the hallway, everyone at church thinks you have a beautiful Christian marriage...

but behind the closed door, one spouse has learned that saying “not tonight,” “I’m hurting,” “I’m exhausted,” “I’m frightened,” or simply “please stop” may bring anger, accusations, manipulation, spiritual pressure, sulking, threats, or punishment?
What happens when someone begins using the Bible not as a lamp...
but as leverage?
This is where Christians must have enough courage to say something clearly:
Marriage creates a profound covenant of sexual faithfulness and mutual belonging.
It does not create unlimited sexual entitlement.
And Scripture itself will not allow us to pretend otherwise.
Go all the way back to the beginning.
Genesis describes marriage with breathtaking language:
וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
vedavaq be'ishto vehayu levasar echad.
A man “clings” or “holds fast” to his wife, and they become “one flesh.”
Basar echad.
One flesh.
Not one human being swallowing another.
Not one will erasing another.
Not one body becoming property to be used regardless of suffering.
Two persons enter a covenantal union so intimate that Scripture describes them as one flesh.
That is sacred.
That is why adultery is devastating.
That is why sexual faithfulness matters.
That is why Christian sexuality cannot be reduced to personal appetite.
And that is precisely why sexual selfishness inside marriage should disturb us too.
Because “one flesh” is not permission to stop seeing the other person.
It is a reason to see them more deeply.
Paul develops this startling mutuality in 1 Corinthians 7.
And this is one of those passages that can become dangerous when someone quotes half of it.
Paul says that a wife does not exercise exclusive authority over her own body, but her husband does.
Someone looking for ammunition might stop there.
But Paul does not.
The Greek continues:
ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ...
“Likewise also...”
And then Paul turns the statement directly around.
The husband does not exercise exclusive authority over his own body either, but his wife does.
Read the symmetry.
Feel the weight of it.
Paul does not write:
He gives neither spouse unilateral bodily sovereignty over the other while preserving unilateral sovereignty for themselves.
The language is reciprocal.
The Greek verb is ἐξουσιάζει — exousiazei — relating to exercising authority.
And Paul deliberately places husband and wife under corresponding obligations.
Then, when he discusses abstaining from sexual relations, he says it should occur:
ἐκ συμφώνου
ek symphōnou.
By agreement.
By mutual consent.
The very passage sometimes dragged into marriages to demand sex actually contains reciprocity and mutual agreement.

Yes, Scripture teaches that husbands and wives should not selfishly weaponize sexual deprivation against each other. Sexual intimacy is a real and important part of marriage. Persistent rejection, manipulation, infidelity, pornography, selfishness, emotional abandonment, and sexual indifference can deeply injure a marriage and should not simply be ignored.
But there is an enormous moral difference between teaching spouses to lovingly give themselves to one another...
and teaching someone that marriage gives them unrestricted access to another human body.
Christian marital intimacy is supposed to be giving.
Not taking.
That difference matters.
Especially to the spouse reading this with tears already forming because nobody ever told them they were allowed to say:
“That hurt.”
“I am afraid.”
“I need you to stop.”
“Something is wrong between us.”
“I need help.”
Maybe you have spent years wondering whether acknowledging your pain somehow makes you a rebellious husband or wife.
Maybe every conversation eventually became the same accusation.
“But the Bible says your body belongs to me.”
Please keep reading.
Because the Bible says something else too.
When Paul describes Christian marriage in Ephesians 5, he does not hand husbands a blank check for selfish domination.
He hands them a cross.
“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.”
The Greek is devastatingly beautiful:
καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.
Christ loved the church...
and gave Himself up for her.
ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν.
He gave Himself.
That is the pattern.
Jesus does not stand before His bride asking, “How much can I extract?”
He gives Himself.
Christian marriage therefore cannot faithfully imitate Christ while making selfish acquisition its governing principle.
A husband is told to love his wife as Christ loved His church. Paul goes even further and tells husbands to love their wives as their own bodies, nourishing and cherishing them.
Think about that.
If she trembles when you touch her, something matters more in that moment than satisfying your desire.
Her trembling matters.
If he is emotionally shattered, his condition matters.
If your spouse is sick, recovering from childbirth, grieving, traumatized, frightened, physically hurting, emotionally overwhelmed, or desperately trying to explain that something feels wrong...
love listens.
Love notices.
Love does not hear “please stop” and begin searching for a Bible verse powerful enough to silence it.
And we need to say something uncomfortable here.
A marriage certificate cannot transform cruelty into Christlikeness.
A wedding ceremony does not baptize selfishness.
Putting the word “biblical” in front of domination does not make domination holy.
And quoting Scripture while disregarding the suffering of the person beside you is not spiritual maturity.
Jesus repeatedly confronted people who knew religious language while missing mercy, justice, faithfulness, and the heart of God.
So perhaps the question Christian spouses should ask in the bedroom is not merely:
“What am I allowed to receive?”
Perhaps there is a much more Christlike question:
“How can I love you?”
That changes everything.
Because Christian sexuality is not supposed to be two people negotiating how much they can take from each other.
It is two covenant partners learning to give themselves faithfully, tenderly, joyfully, truthfully, and sacrificially.
Sometimes that giving looks like passionate intimacy.
Sometimes it looks like waiting.
Sometimes it looks like asking, “Are you okay?”
Sometimes it looks like holding someone without expecting sex afterward.
Sometimes it means confessing selfishness.
Sometimes it means confronting persistent rejection rather than pretending everything is fine.
Sometimes it means counseling.
Sometimes it means medical care.
Sometimes it means exposing abuse that has been hidden beneath religious language.
And sometimes the most Christian sentence spoken in a bedroom may simply be:
“I love you more than I love getting what I want tonight.”
That sounds remarkably close to the shape of the cross.
This truth also cuts both ways.
A wife should not manipulate her husband sexually.
A husband should not manipulate his wife sexually.
Neither spouse should use affection as currency.
Neither should deliberately humiliate the other.
Neither should weaponize Scripture.
Neither should treat the other's body as an appliance for personal gratification.
Neither should use prolonged withholding as revenge or coercion.
Neither should assume that being married eliminates the need for tenderness, communication, patience, repentance, and mutual care.
Biblical mutuality does not mean sexual demands become irrelevant.
It means those needs are handled inside love rather than domination.
There may be someone reading this who has been the hurting spouse.
But there may also be someone reading this who suddenly realizes:
I have been the one doing the hurting.
Don't run from that realization.
Run to Christ with it.
Maybe you never considered yourself abusive.
Maybe you thought pressure was normal.
Maybe you confused leadership with control.
Maybe you believed marriage meant your spouse could never refuse you.
Maybe you became angry when intimacy did not happen.
Maybe you punished your spouse emotionally afterward.
Maybe you quoted 1 Corinthians 7 while conveniently forgetting that the same chapter speaks reciprocally.
Maybe your spouse eventually stopped arguing.
And you called the silence peace.
But silence is not always peace.
Sometimes silence is what happens when somebody has given up believing they will be heard.
If that realization cuts you...
do not waste the wound.
Repent.
Not the cheap repentance that says, “I'm sorry you felt that way.”
Real repentance.
“I sinned against you.”
“I used pressure where I should have shown love.”
“I cared more about getting what I wanted than understanding what you were experiencing.”
“I used Scripture selfishly.”
“I frightened you.”
“Will you forgive me?”
And then accept that forgiveness cannot be demanded on your timetable either.
Repentance bears fruit.
It changes behavior.
It welcomes accountability.
It stops hiding.
It stops defending what Christ is exposing.
Because this is where the Gospel enters the room.
Not as decoration.
Not as a religious excuse.
As rescue.
Christianity is not the story of righteous people successfully hiding their scandals.
It is the story of sinners being exposed by holiness and then offered mercy through Jesus Christ.
Christ died for sexual sinners.
Christ died for selfish spouses.
Christ died for adulterers.
Christ died for people drowning in pornography.
Christ died for manipulators.
Christ died for the ashamed.
Christ died for the wounded.
Christ died for those who have committed sins they desperately wish they could erase.
And Christ is able to transform people who truly come to Him in repentance and faith.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace brings darkness into the light and refuses to leave us there.
That is why repentance and grace belong together.
Grace without truth becomes permission.
Truth without grace becomes condemnation.
But at Calvary we see both.
Our sin was serious enough that Christ died.
His mercy was great enough that Christ willingly died for sinners.
That is scandalous grace.
And perhaps that is why this subject matters so much.
Because the bedroom is one of the places where Christians can become extraordinarily skilled at pretending.
Nobody at church sees it.
Nobody in the Bible study knows.
Nobody watching the smiling family photograph understands what happened fifteen minutes before it was taken.
But Jesus sees.
He sees the spouse crying quietly in the bathroom.
He sees the husband terrified to admit that something in his marriage is broken.
He sees the wife who has confused endurance with holiness.
He sees the spouse whose selfishness has been protected by theology.
He sees the shame.
He sees the secrets.
He sees the wounds.
And He also sees what redemption could become.

If you are experiencing sexual coercion, violence, threats, or abuse, seeking safety and trustworthy help is not a betrayal of Scripture. Serious harm should not be hidden merely to preserve appearances. Reach out to appropriate local emergency services when immediate danger exists and to trustworthy pastoral, professional, legal, medical, or domestic-abuse support as appropriate to your situation.
And if you are the spouse causing fear...
stop.
Do not demand another chance while continuing the behavior.
Do not demand secrecy.
Do not demand instant forgiveness.
Bring what you have done into the light.
Seek serious pastoral and professional accountability.
Repent before God.
Accept consequences.
Learn what Christlike love actually looks like.
Because Jesus did not save us so we could become more sophisticated at defending our sin.
He saves sinners to transform them.
This is where “From Scandal to Grace” becomes more than a slogan.
Your scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
Your wound does not have to become your identity.
Your worst sin does not have to become the last sentence written over your life.
Your marriage may need help.
Your theology may need correction.
Your heart may need repentance.
Your wounds may need years of healing.
Your situation may require difficult decisions and wise counsel rather than simplistic internet advice.
But Jesus Christ still specializes in resurrection.
Dead things are not intimidating to the One who walked out of a grave.
So bring Him the truth.
Not the Instagram marriage.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the cleaned-up testimony.
The truth.
“Jesus, this is what happened.”
“Jesus, this is what I did.”
“Jesus, this is what was done to me.”
“Jesus, this is what I became.”
“Jesus, I need mercy.”
There is grace at the cross.
Not permission to continue hurting people.
Grace to become different.
Grace to confess.
Grace to forgive where forgiveness is possible.
Grace to establish truth.
Grace to pursue safety.
Grace to rebuild what can faithfully be rebuilt.
Grace to stop pretending.
Grace to repent.
Grace to heal.
Grace to become more like Jesus.
And maybe this article needs to travel farther than your screen.
There is probably a husband who needs to read it before selfishness destroys tenderness in his marriage.
There may be a wife who has spent years believing God requires her to silently endure what God never called holy.
There may be a newlywed couple who need to understand this before harmful patterns become normal.

There may be a pastor, counselor, father, mother, son, daughter, friend, struggling believer, seeker, lukewarm Christian, or even an unbeliever who needs to discover that biblical Christianity is not a license for sexual selfishness.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedient love, truth, mercy, holiness, generosity, and service.

But if this truth can protect a marriage, expose hidden sin, comfort somebody suffering in silence, or lead one person toward repentance and Jesus Christ, sharing it can become one small act of putting useful truth into someone else's path.
Let the comments become more than engagement.
Let them become evidence that Christians can tell the truth without pretending to have perfect lives.
Not because money purchases spiritual blessing.
And never because the Gospel is for sale.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
But Gospel work can be supported.
Because somebody in your circle may never tell you what is happening behind their bedroom door.
Somebody may read silently.
Somebody may cry.
Somebody may finally ask for help.
Somebody may finally repent.
Somebody may discover that the Bible they thought condemned them actually points them toward the crucified and risen Christ.
And somebody may finally understand that Christian marriage was never meant to make one spouse the possession of another.
It was meant to become a living witness to covenant faithfulness, sacrificial love, truth, holiness, tenderness, forgiveness, and the astonishing love of Jesus Christ.
A ring can tell the world that you are married.
But only the way you love when nobody is watching reveals what you believe marriage is for.
And when selfishness, shame, wounds, and hidden sins have already written pages you wish could disappear, remember this:
Jesus is not frightened by the chapter you are ashamed to let anyone read. Give Him the pen.
